newsitem.title: switzerland: FOCUS-Nestle sees good 1997 profit growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nestle sees good 1997 profit growth.

text.p: Nestle SA chairman Helmut Maucher forecast on Tuesday that the world's biggest food company would post double-digit gains in sales and profit in 1997 after a weak Swiss franc helped to boost first quarter turnover by 18.7 percent.
"We are looking forward probably to a double-digit growth in sales and profits," he told Reuters Financial Television.

"We are expecting a very good year and this year of course the currency should help us," he added after his last appearance as chief executive at Nestle's annual news conference. Maucher steps down in June but remains chairman.

His remarks helped Nestle shares bounce back from early losses as dealers focused on the scant 2.2 percent rise in sales volume in the first quarter. Shares hit a low of 1,795 Swiss francs, down 47 francs, before recovering to close down 40 at 1,802 in afternoon trading.
First quarter group sales hit 16.1 billion francs ($10.9 billion), Nestle said, adding that initial April data confirmed the growth trend.

The Swiss franc's decline against major currencies, especially in the second half of 1996, contributed the lion's share of the sales growth in the first quarter, although volumes accelerated during March, it said.

"Nestle expects good growth in both consolidated sales and consolidated net profit for the whole of the year. It is clear, however, that the rhythm of growth will diminish in the course of the second semester, since the foreign exchange comparison will be established on a less favourable base," Nestle said.

Net monetary factors accounted for 15.7 percentage points of the first quarter sales rise. Of this, price increases accounted for 2.7 points and exchange rates moves made up 13.0 points. The net effect of acquisitions and disposals was 0.8 point.
In 1996 Nestle's sales grew 7.1 percent to 60.49 billion francs. Net profit rose 16.6 percent to a record 3.40 billion.
Dealers said they were disappointed by the results in the first three months, which fell short of market expectations that turnover could swell 20 percent or more.
"We were less disappointed by the sales growth than by volume growth, which was only 2.2 percent instead of the three percent that the experts had expected," one dealer at a big Swiss bank said.
"I can imagine that several banks will now reduce their earnings estimates slightly for Nestle," he added.
Maucher said he was also disappointed by the 2.2 percent figure, but added he was confident volume growth would exceed four percent for 1997. Volume in March rose 4.7 percent.
"Our estimate for the year is 4.7 percent," Maucher said, adding: "I am rather certain it (sales volume growth) will be over four percent, which is our goal."
Another dealer said the stock market, already in a skittish mood, was ready to punish any disappointing results.

Finance chief Mario Corti's statement that Nestle was not considering any share buyback scheme, as many other Swiss companies have launched, also weighed on its share price, dealers said, although Maucher had often said this in the past.
Its refusal to consider selling off its minority stake in French cosmetics giant L'Oreal or its Alcon pharmaceuticals division also encouraged bears.

In nearly 16 years as chief executive, Maucher has built Nestle into a global power that diversified from its traditional reliance on instant coffee and chocolate into new markets and products like ice cream and mineral water with great potential.
He said Nestle was happy with its current stake in L'Oreal, but envisaged getting a majority and uniting it in a holding company grouping the world's biggest food and cosmetics groups.

Nestle has a 49 percent stake in Gesparal, the company that controls L'Oreal. The Bettencourt family owns the other 51 percent stake. Maucher said he did not expect the family to sell it soon, but added that the partners were open to discussions.
He made clear that L'Oreal would remain an independent company even if Nestle were eventually able to acquire a majority.
